highlights.text: whose core notion is **putting at a distance, driving away**
طَرَدْتُهُ ṭaradtuhu — "I drove him away."
With the ruler as subject, forms IV and II (أَطْرَدَهُ / طَرَّدَهُ) mean to banish someone from his town
Do you recognise a trace, like the running-on of streaked patterns, belonging to ʿAmra — desolate, save for a rider's halting-place?
treats b-r-d as having four independent bases, with all derived forms tracing back to one of them
barada / bārid: to be cold, cold.
saḥāb barid: a cloud carrying hail (barad).
a verse promises a she-camel that "will cool livers and set mourners weeping."
evidenced by a verse on gazelles pillowed on the arṭā bush's "two cool sides."
treats d-n-w as nearness (al-dunūw = al-qurb), whether nearness in essence or nearness in status and judgement
The palm tree's "clusters hanging near" (qinwān dāniya, Q 6:99) show the plain sense.
**First**, against "last": al-dunyā against al-ākhira
adnā means it is nearer, for their own souls, to aiming at justice in testifying
In the saying "when you eat, fa-dannū", al-Rāghib derives the word from al-dūn ("what is near/below"), giving the sense "eat from what is next to you"
treats j-d-r as two independent roots
جِدَار (jidār) = a wall; plurals جُدُر (judur) and جُدْرَان (judrān)
هو جَدِيرٌ بكذا (huwa jadīrun bi-kadhā), "he is fit/worthy of it,"
derives every sense of the root ج-ل-س (j-l-s) from one core meaning: rising/elevation (al-irtifāʿ)
jalasa describes the transition from lying down or sleep into a sitting position
several lines of poetry (al-Hudhalī and others) using jalasa/al-jālis in this "went up to Najd" sense
turns on "coming into being / being brought forth" and, from that, "growing up."
"God brought creation forth (anshaʾa), so it came to be (nashaʾū)."
Qur'anic phrase "الجوار المنشآت" — the running ships with sails hoisted.
with the Qur'anic phrase "من ينشّؤا في الحلية" ("one reared amid ornament")
A verse of al-Shammākh uses mustanshaʾāt ("raised-up things") of howdah-like shapes
a single sound root whose core sense is: striking something until a dent or hollow is beaten into it
naqīr: the small speck on the back of a date-stone
He cites a woman's saying to her husband: take me past the men of naẓarā (who look) but not past the women of naqarā (who backbite)
God would not leave off from the slayer of a believer, i.e. not desist from punishing him
قَصَا – يَقْصُو – قُصُوّاً is to move away or stand apart, said of anything
القاصية (al-qāṣiya) describes both people and places that are remote and set apart
Ruʾba: "it leaves the soil of the deserts with its dust-clouds driven wild."
hanging something on something so that it stays attached to it
a share, a portion
taqlīd — putting a mark on the neck.
maqālīd — said to mean treasuries or storehouses
Ibn Fāris cites the poet Bishr: "Your patron bestowed it on you out of rancour — and Jaʿfar was collared with it as with a dove's ring-collar."
sets out three genuine base-meanings for this root
Ibn Fāris cites Qur'an 22:21, "wa-lahum maqāmiʿu min ḥadīd" ("for them are maces of iron")
He quotes the pre-Islamic/early poet Aws (ibn Ḥajar): God sent down His help, while the dust-colored gazelles in their lairs go on warding off flies (taqammaʿu).
A ḥadīth calls certain people "the funnels of speech" (aqmāʿ al-qawl): those who hear but retain nothing, as if their ears were funnels that hold nothing back
whose single idea is: mingling with a thing, getting entangled in it, and putting it on like a garment
اقْتَرَفَ (iqtarafa) = to acquire or gain something
a people complained of the pestilence of their land and were told, "Move away, for from al-qaraf comes destruction."
two sound root meanings: cold, and firm establishment (settling in place)
Qarra and istaqarra: to settle, to become settled
may God give him enough that his eye rests and does not look longingly to anyone above him
Imruʾ al-Qays: "when they mount the horses and put on their mail, the earth burns, though the day is cold (qarr)."
a single consistent root meaning breadth/spaciousness and moving out freely across the land
سَرَب / سَرِب (sarab, sarib) — water leaking or flowing from a water-skin
سَارِب (sārib) — one going forth openly in the land
Shāhid: Dhū al-Rumma, "What ails your eye that water pours from it, as though it were a leak from the split seams of a water-skin"
sāḥa al-māʾ describes water flowing/streaming over the ground
sāḥa fī al-arḍ means to travel or roam through the land (siyāḥa)
Al-Zamakhshari cites the Qur'anic phrase "so travel/roam through the land" as the model usage
A verse attributed to Abu Talib is quoted about the sāʾiḥīn tasting no drop for their Lord's sake (the second half of the line is textually uncertain
to join/connect one thing to another (waṣala … fa-ttaṣala, "he joined it, and it became joined")
Form II waṣṣala (tawṣīl) = to splice or link repeatedly; cited with Qurʾān 28:51, "We have joined together the discourse for them."
a ewe that "accompanied"/was paired with her brother among the flock's young and so was spared slaughter
ittaṣala / waṣala ilā a tribe = to attach oneself, claim lineage (verse of al-Aʿshā)
khaṭṭa al-kitāb — to write a document
wa lā takhuṭṭuhu bi-yamīnika" — "nor did you write it with your right hand"
illustrated with a line of poetry by al-Nābighah about an unmatched rival at the Battle of ʿUkāẓ
derives the whole root خ-ب-ط from one core idea: treading and striking
the verb يَتَخَبَّطُ here carries the same "being struck/buffeted" image
treats خ-ر-ق as a single root meaning to tear something open and to cut/pass through it
The poet Dhū al-Khiraq al-Ṭuhawī got his name from his line "upon it are the feathers and the rags."
An Arab saying: "She has neither a height that disparages her nor a shortness that abashes her"
al-yaqīn is knowledge that removes doubt and settles a matter as certain — the opposite of doubt, as knowledge is the opposite of ignorance
all meaning "to be/become certain of a matter"
al-yaqan = al-yaqīn, with a shāhid from al-Aʿshā
glossed as "until death comes to you," i.e. worship Him always, to the point of death
z-h-q as one root meaning: to move forward, to pass on, to go past a limit
زَهَقَتْ نَفْسُهُ — "his soul departed."
زَهَقَ الْبَاطِلُ — falsehood zahaqa, glossed by him simply as "it passed away, went off."
Shāhid from Zuhayr, contrasting the mounts of a war-leader: "among them the lean and among them the fat, grease-laden (al-zāhiq al-zahim)."
